query: Consider the following context: Temper embrittlement, characterized by a dramatic loss of ductility within a narrow temperature window, is ubiquitous in conventional alloys but is not reported in compositionally complex or high‐entropy alloy systems. In that context, which material can be used for ductile–brittle–ductile transition, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A deliberately compositionally modified AlCoCrFeNi-based high‐entropy alloy, when doped with a minor amount of an embrittlement‐promoting element (e.g., Cu) and subjected to a tailored thermal treatment, can display a ductile–brittle–ductile transition in a narrow temperature range.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single-phase AlCoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy prepared via arc‐melting (or similar synthesis) that normally shows uniformly ductile behavior with no temper embrittlement.
generation.intervention: Introduce a small (approximately 1 at.%) concentration of a temper embrittlement–promoting element and apply precise heat treatments in the temperature window corresponding to the conventional temper embrittlement regime.
generation.conditions: Experiments carried out over a narrow temperature range that spans from room temperature to above the embrittlement regime; controlled annealing and cooling cycles to promote controlled grain-boundary segregation.
generation.structural_mediator: Localized solute segregation at the grain boundaries emerging as a result of the modified composition and specific heat treatment.
generation.mechanism: The minor embrittlement‐promoting element is expected to segregate to the grain boundaries during annealing, inducing a brittle phase or weakening the intergranular cohesion in a specific intermediate temperature range. At lower and higher temperatures, either the segregation is not activated or is dissolved, restoring ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy will exhibit high ductility at low temperatures, a significant drop in ductility (and corresponding increase in brittle fracture tendencies) in a narrow intermediate temperature regime, and a recovery of ductility at higher temperatures.
generation.baseline: Conventional homogeneous high‐entropy AlCoCrFeNi alloys which do not exhibit any temper embrittlement behavior.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected only for a specific window of dopant concentration and heat treatment conditions; variations outside this window may not trigger sufficient segregation and thus fail to produce the ductile–brittle–ductile transition.
generation.uncertainty: The exact dopant concentration required and precise temperature boundaries for the ductile–brittle–ductile behavior are not well established and need experimental determination.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two alloy batches: one standard AlCoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy and one modified version with ~1 at.% a selected embrittlement‐promoting element (e.g., Cu). Subject both sets to identical controlled heat treatments within the temper embrittlement temperature range. Conduct tensile tests and fracture analyses across a temperature sweep spanning below, within, and above the expected embrittlement regime.
measurements: Fractography to identify brittle versus ductile fracture features
Grain boundary compositional analysis (e.g., via SEM-EDS or TEM) to detect segregated phases
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified (doped) alloy does not show a statistically significant dip in ductility (or corresponding increase in brittle fracture markers) during the intermediate temperature range, compared to the control alloy, then the hypothesis that the dopant-induced segregation drives a ductile–brittle–ductile transition is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High entropy or compositionally complex alloys provide opportunities for optimization towards new high-temperature materials. Improvements in the equiatomic alloy Al 17 Co 17 Cr 17 Cu 17 Fe 17 Ni 17 (at.%) led to the base alloy for this work with the chemical composition Al 10 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 (at.%). Characterization of the beneficial particle-strengthened microstructure by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and observation of good mechanical properties at elevated temperatures arose the need of accomplishing further optimization steps. For this purpose, the refractory metals hafnium and molybdenum were added in small amounts (0.5 and 1.0 at.% respectively) because of their well-known positive effects on mechanical properties of Ni-based superalloys. By correlation of microstructural examinations using SEM with tensile tests in the temperature range of room temperature up to 900 °C, conclusions could be drawn for further optimization steps. Keywords: HEA, high entropy alloys, compositionally complex alloys, mechanical characterization

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) present a new approach of alloying concepts. Whereas conventional alloys usually comprise one major alloying element and minor additions of other alloying elements to improve properties, HEAs consist of at least five elements with close to equimolar composition. For several compositions, the desired formation of solely solid solutions with a face-centred cubic (fcc) or a body-centred cubic (bcc) structure could be achieved [ [1] , [2] , [3] ].

Several groups of HEAs have been intensively investigated. The term compositionally complex alloys (CCAs) was introduced for HEAs with a multiphase microstructure [ [4] ]. Several investigations prove the formation of primarily cubic phases in the alloy AlCoCrCuFeNi and its derivatives [ [5] , [6] , [7] ]. Aluminium strongly influences the microstructure, phase formation and resulting properties. Furthermore, aluminium acts as a stabiliser of bcc solid solutions and can suppress the formation of complex phases [ [8] , [9] , [10] ]. chosen.technique: alloy synthesis via arc‐melting combined with tailored heat treatments and mechanical testing
chosen.conditions: performing experiments in the narrow temperature range where temper embrittlement is known to occur in conventional alloys, but now applied to a compositionally complex (or high‐entropy) alloy with adjusted elemental ratios to trigger controlled segregation
chosen.why: Previous work has not reported temper embrittlement in high‐entropy or compositionally complex alloys, likely because their intrinsic compositional homogeneity suppresses segregation. By deliberately modifying the composition to include a minor embrittlement‐promoting element and applying precise thermal treatments, the study directly addresses the open question by seeking a ductile–brittle–ductile transition. This experimental approach both fills the identified gap and uses well‐established alloy design and mechanical testing techniques typical for the field.
